analogy.p: The **nucleus** is the head office holding the master plans (DNA). The **ribosomes** are the machines on the factory floor that build products (proteins) from the plans. The **mitochondria** are the power station, releasing energy so everything can run. The **cell membrane** is the security gate controlling what goes in and out, and the **cytoplasm** is the factory floor where the work happens. In a plant factory there is also a **cell wall** (strong outer walls), a **vacuole** (a big water tank that keeps the building firm) and **chloroplasts** (solar panels that capture light). It breaks down because a factory’s power station makes its own electricity, whereas mitochondria only **release** energy stored in glucose, and cells make and repair their own parts.

bullets: **Both animal and plant cells**: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes.
**Plant cells only**: cell wall (cellulose), permanent vacuole (cell sap), chloroplasts (in the green parts).
You must be able to **link structure to function**, e.g. many mitochondria in a muscle cell because muscle needs a lot of energy.
You must know that animal and plant cells are **eukaryotic**.
You should know which structures can be seen with a **light microscope** and which need an **electron microscope**.
Typical marks: 1 mark for naming a function, 2 to 3 marks for "explain" with a reason.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA requires you to **recognise, name and describe** the main sub-cellular structures in **animal and plant cells** and to **explain how each structure is related to its function**. The structures named in the specification are the **nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes** (in all cells) and the **cell wall, permanent vacuole and chloroplasts** (in plant cells). Exam questions are usually a labelled diagram, "state the function of X" or "explain why this cell has many of Y".

bullets: Contains **genetic material (DNA)** arranged in **chromosomes**.
**Controls the activities of the cell** because genes code for proteins (including enzymes) that determine what the cell does.
Is **enclosed by a nuclear membrane** (that is what makes the cell eukaryotic).
Is where **DNA is copied** before the cell divides.
Appears as a **round or oval structure**, often stained darker under a light microscope.
**Red blood cells** are an example of a specialised cell with **no nucleus** (more room for haemoglobin).
Do not say the nucleus "controls the cell" without mentioning DNA/genes.
core.p: The **nucleus** is the control centre of the cell. It contains the cell’s **genetic material (DNA)**, which is organised into **chromosomes**, and it **controls the activities of the cell** by determining which proteins are made. The nucleus is usually the largest sub-cellular structure and is surrounded by a **nuclear membrane** with tiny pores that allow instructions to leave. In an exam, the answer "controls the cell" must be backed up with "contains the DNA/genes".

bullets: **Site of most chemical reactions** in the cell.
Contains **enzymes** that speed up these reactions.
**Holds** the organelles (mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts) in place.
Is mostly **water** with dissolved nutrients, ions and proteins.
Is found in **all** cells: animal, plant and bacterial.
In plant cells, the cytoplasm is squashed against the cell wall by the large vacuole.
Do not confuse cytoplasm with **cell sap**, which is inside the vacuole.
core.p: The **cytoplasm** is a **gel-like substance** that fills the cell between the cell membrane and the nucleus. It is where **most of the chemical reactions** needed for life take place, which is why it contains many **enzymes** and dissolved substances. It also holds the other sub-cellular structures in place. Many students lose marks by saying cytoplasm "holds the cell together" or is just "jelly"; the key idea is **chemical reactions**.

bullets: **Controls what enters and leaves** the cell.
**Partially permeable**: allows small molecules such as oxygen through easily.
Substances cross by **diffusion, osmosis and active transport**.
Found in **animal, plant and bacterial** cells.
In plant cells it lies **just inside the cell wall**.
Do not say the membrane "keeps the cell shape": that is the **cell wall** (plants) or the cytoskeleton.
The membrane is **not** a barrier that nothing gets through.
core.p: The **cell membrane** surrounds the cytoplasm and **controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell**. It is **partially (selectively) permeable**: it lets some substances through, such as oxygen, water and some nutrients, and keeps others in or out. Substances cross by **diffusion, osmosis and active transport** (see the transport topics). It is very thin, so it cannot be seen with a light microscope as a separate structure.

bullets: Site of **aerobic respiration**, which **releases energy** for the cell.
Word equation: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water** (energy released).
**Many mitochondria** in: muscle cells, sperm cells (tail), nerve cells, liver cells and root hair cells (active transport).
Found in **both animal and plant cells** (plants respire all the time too).
**Not** found in bacteria.
The inner membrane is folded to give a **larger surface area** for respiration reactions.
Never say mitochondria "make energy": energy cannot be made, it is **transferred (released)**.
core.p: **Mitochondria** (singular: mitochondrion) are the sites of **aerobic respiration**, the reaction that releases **energy** from glucose using oxygen. Many of the reactions of respiration are controlled by enzymes found on the folded inner membrane, whose large surface area allows more reactions to happen. The energy released is used for **muscle contraction, active transport, making large molecules and keeping the body warm**. Cells that need a lot of energy contain **many mitochondria**.

bullets: Site of **protein synthesis** (making proteins from amino acids).
Found in **animal, plant and bacterial** cells.
Too small to see with a **light microscope**; seen with an **electron microscope**.
Proteins made include **enzymes**, hormones and structural proteins such as collagen.
Cells that make a lot of protein (e.g. gland cells making enzymes) have **many ribosomes**.
Link: the **nucleus** holds the genes, the **ribosome** builds the protein.
Do not say ribosomes "make energy" or "make proteins in the nucleus".
core.p: **Ribosomes** are tiny structures where **protein synthesis** takes place. They read the instructions copied from the genes and join amino acids together in the correct order to make proteins such as enzymes and structural proteins. They can be found free in the cytoplasm or attached to membranes. They are so small that they can only be seen using an **electron microscope**. They are found in **all** cell types, including bacteria.

bullets: Made of **cellulose** fibres.
**Strengthens** the cell and **supports** the plant.
Lies **outside** the cell membrane.
Is **fully permeable** (it does not control what enters).
Stops the cell **bursting** when water enters by osmosis.
**Not** present in animal cells.
Bacteria also have a cell wall, but it is **not made of cellulose**.
core.p: The **cell wall** of a plant cell is made of **cellulose** and lies **outside the cell membrane**. It is rigid and **strengthens the cell and supports the plant**. Because it is fully permeable, water and dissolved substances pass through it easily; the control of what enters the cell is done by the membrane beneath it. The wall stops the cell bursting when it takes in a lot of water by osmosis, producing a firm, **turgid** cell.

bullets: Contains **cell sap** (a solution of sugars and ions).
Helps keep the cell **turgid** (firm), which **supports the plant**.
Is **permanent**: it is always present in a mature plant cell (animal cells can have only small temporary vacuoles).
Takes up much of the cell in many plant cells.
Cell sap is **not** the cytoplasm.
If a plant loses water, the vacuole shrinks and the cell becomes **flaccid**, so the plant wilts.
Found in plant cells, **not** in animal cells.
core.p: The **permanent vacuole** is a large space in the middle of a mature plant cell filled with **cell sap**, a solution of **sugars, mineral ions and other substances** in water. It is surrounded by a membrane. Its role is to **keep the cell turgid** and to help support the plant by pushing the cytoplasm against the cell wall. It also stores dissolved materials.

bullets: Site of **photosynthesis**.
Contain **chlorophyll**, which **absorbs light**.
Word equation: **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen** (using light energy).
Found in **leaf cells and other green parts** of plants.
**Not** found in root cells or animal cells.
**Palisade cells** have lots of chloroplasts so they absorb more light.
Plant cells have **both** chloroplasts and mitochondria.
core.p: **Chloroplasts** are the sites of **photosynthesis**. They contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which **absorbs light energy** needed to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Chloroplasts are found in the **green parts** of the plant, mainly in the leaf (especially the palisade mesophyll cells). Root cells do not have chloroplasts because they are underground and receive no light.

bullets: **Both**: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes.
**Plant only**: **cell wall, permanent vacuole, chloroplasts**.
Plant cells are usually **regular in shape** (rigid wall); animal cells often have **irregular shapes**.
Plant cells store **starch**; animal cells store **glycogen** (where stated).
Both are **eukaryotic**.
Neither type has a flagellum as a normal feature in this spec.
Only **green parts** of plants contain chloroplasts, so not every plant cell has them.
core.p: Animal and plant cells share the same basic eukaryotic structures, and the plant cell has three **extra** structures that suit a lifestyle based on photosynthesis and a fixed, supported body. Exam answers should list similarities and differences with comparative words. A common 3-mark question asks for the structures found in a plant cell but **not** in an animal cell.

bullets: **Eukaryotic cell:** has a **nucleus** that contains the genetic material (animal, plant, fungal and algal cells).
**Prokaryotic cell:** has **no nucleus**; the DNA is a **single loop** in the cytoplasm.
Prokaryotic cells are usually **much smaller** than eukaryotic cells.
Both types have **cytoplasm, a cell membrane and ribosomes**.
**Mitochondria and chloroplasts** are found in eukaryotic cells; bacteria carry out respiration without mitochondria.
Plant and algal cell walls are made of **cellulose**; bacterial cell walls are made of a different substance.
If an exam asks 'give one difference between a plant cell and a bacterial cell', use **'plant cell has a nucleus; bacterial DNA is not in a nucleus'**.
Use the word **'sub-cellular structures'** for the parts inside any cell.
core.h: Eukaryotic cells compared with prokaryotic cells
core.p: Animal and plant cells are both **eukaryotic cells**, which means their genetic material is enclosed in a **nucleus**. **Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria) are much smaller and have **no nucleus**; their DNA is a single loop floating free in the cytoplasm, sometimes with extra small rings called plasmids. Prokaryotes still have cytoplasm, a cell membrane, a cell wall (not made of cellulose) and ribosomes. Knowing this contrast helps you answer questions that ask which structures are specific to animal, plant or bacterial cells.

bullets: **Many mitochondria** → more aerobic respiration → more energy released → for muscle contraction/active transport.
**Many chloroplasts** (palisade cell) → more chlorophyll → absorb more light → more photosynthesis.
**Many ribosomes** (gland cell) → more protein synthesis → more enzymes made.
**No chloroplasts** in root cells → no light underground.
**Large permanent vacuole** → keeps cell turgid → supports non-woody plants.
**No nucleus** in a red blood cell → more room for haemoglobin → carries more oxygen.
Use the sentence frame: "It has many X, which do Y, so the cell can Z."
core.p: The grade 9 skill is **explaining why** a cell has more of one structure. Always follow the chain: **structure → function → benefit to the cell**. For example, a muscle cell needs a lot of energy to contract, so it has many mitochondria to carry out aerobic respiration and release energy. A root hair cell needs energy for active transport of mineral ions, so it has many mitochondria but no chloroplasts because it is underground.

bullets: **Light microscope**: cheaper, portable, can view **living** specimens, lower magnification and resolution.
**Electron microscope**: expensive, large, specimens are usually **dead** and prepared in a vacuum, much higher magnification and resolution.
**Resolution** is the ability to see two close objects as **separate**.
**Magnification** = image size ÷ real size.
Ribosomes are only visible using an **electron microscope**.
The development of the electron microscope **allowed understanding of sub-cellular structures** in much finer detail.
See the microscopy notes (bio.0.2) for magnification calculations.
core.p: A **light microscope** can show the **nucleus, cell wall, permanent vacuole and chloroplasts**, and the cytoplasm as a granular background. An **electron microscope** has much higher **magnification and resolution**, so it can show smaller sub-cellular structures: **ribosomes, the internal structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts** and plasmids. This is why our detailed knowledge of cells has increased since the electron microscope was developed.

bullets: Label lines must **touch** the structure and never cross.
Write **cell membrane**, **cell wall**, **permanent vacuole**: use full names.
Draw **mitochondria** as small oval shapes with an inner fold.
Draw **chloroplasts** as small green ovals (colour them or label them).
Draw the **nucleus** as a round structure inside the cytoplasm.
Add a **title** and, if asked, a **scale** or magnification.
Do not draw chloroplasts in an animal cell, or a cell wall in an animal cell.
core.p: Diagram marks are given for correct structure names, correct position and clear label lines. Use a sharp pencil, a ruler for the lines, and make sure each line ends on the structure and not near it. Draw plant cells with straight sides and a thick wall, and animal cells with rounded irregular outlines. Always check the number of structures you are asked to name.

bullets: **magnification = image size / real size** (the equation in the specification).
Rearranged: **real size = image size / magnification** and **image size = magnification x real size**.
Measure the image with a **ruler in mm**, then convert to um by multiplying by 1000.
Worked check: image 40 mm, magnification x400 gives real size 0.1 mm = **100 um**.
Magnification has **no units**; the image and real size must use the same unit.
**Standard form** is used for very small sizes, e.g. 0.000 002 m = 2 x 10^-6 m.
A scale bar shows a known real length: real size = (image length / scale bar image length) x scale bar value.
Check your answer: a plant cell is about 100 um, an animal cell about 10 to 30 um.
core.p: Microscope questions often ask you to find the real size of a structure from a drawing or photograph. Use the equation **magnification = image size / real size**, and rearrange it to **real size = image size / magnification**. Before you substitute, convert every length to the **same unit**: 1 mm = 1000 micrometres (um) and 1 um = 1000 nanometres (nm). Examiners award a mark for the correct rearrangement, a mark for unit conversion and a mark for the final answer with its unit.

exam: **1 mark (state a function)**: use the spec wording, e.g. "site of aerobic respiration" for mitochondria; avoid vague words like "powerhouse" on their own.
**Name the structure from a description**: match the key words: gel/reactions = cytoplasm; protein synthesis = ribosomes; contains chlorophyll = chloroplast.
**2 marks (Explain why a cell has many X)**: structure → function → reason, e.g. many mitochondria, so more aerobic respiration, so more energy released for muscle contraction.
**3 mark (Plant vs animal)**: name all three extras (cell wall, permanent vacuole, chloroplasts) and say which cell has them.
**Diagram questions**: use the exact label names; avoid "membrane" alone if there is also a nuclear membrane or wall.
**Microscope questions**: ribosomes need an **electron microscope** because of its higher resolution; do not say "it is bigger".
**Equation recall**: respiration glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; photosynthesis carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
**Application questions**: if the cell is underground (root), expect **no chloroplasts**; if it is very active, expect **many mitochondria**.
**4 marks**: for compare questions use "whereas" and mention at least one similarity and one difference.
**Command words**: State (short), Describe (say what), Explain (because), Suggest (apply your knowledge).
**Data**: if given counts of organelles per cell, compare the **numbers** and link the biggest to the cell’s function.
**Magnification (3 marks)**: write the equation, convert units (mm to um) and give the answer with a unit, e.g. 40 / 400 = 0.1 mm = 100 um.

mistakes.r: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose; energy is transferred, not made.
The cell membrane controls this; the cellulose cell wall strengthens and supports the cell.
mistakes.w: The cell wall controls what enters and leaves the cell.

mistakes.r: All cells have a cell membrane; animal cells just lack a cell wall.
mistakes.w: Animal cells have no membrane because they have no cell wall.

mistakes.r: Plants do both: mitochondria for respiration and chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
mistakes.w: Plants do not respire because they photosynthesise (so no mitochondria).

mistakes.r: Only in green parts, e.g. leaf cells; root cells have none.
mistakes.w: Chloroplasts are in all plant cells.

mistakes.r: The nucleus contains the genetic material (DNA) that controls the activities of the cell.
mistakes.w: The nucleus controls the cell. (no reason)

mistakes.r: The permanent vacuole contains cell sap (sugars and ions) and helps keep the cell turgid.
mistakes.w: The vacuole stores water and food as starch.

mistakes.r: Ribosomes are where protein synthesis happens, in the cytoplasm.
mistakes.w: Ribosomes make energy / are in the nucleus.

mistakes.r: Chloroplasts are only in the green, light-exposed parts (e.g. leaf cells); root cells have none.
mistakes.w: Chloroplasts are found in all plant cells.

summary: AQA 4.1.1.2: you must name the sub-cellular structures of animal and plant cells (nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes; plus cell wall, permanent vacuole and chloroplasts in plant cells) and explain how each is related to its function. It is the foundation for specialised cells, transport, respiration and photosynthesis.

terms.d: Contains the genetic material that controls the activities of the cell.
A gel-like substance where most of the chemical reactions happen.
Controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
Sub-cellular structures where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy.
Tiny structures where protein synthesis takes place.
A rigid structure made of cellulose that strengthens the cell and supports the plant.
A space in a plant cell filled with cell sap that helps keep the cell turgid.
Contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
The solution of sugars and mineral ions in the permanent vacuole.
Respiration using oxygen that releases energy from glucose: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Reaction that makes glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water using light energy.
Swollen and firm because the cell is full of water and pushing against the cell wall.
A cell with genetic material enclosed in a nucleus; animal and plant cells are eukaryotic.
A part of a cell with a specific function (also called an organelle).
Allowing some substances to pass through but not others.
A tough carbohydrate that makes up the cell walls of plant and algal cells; it strengthens the cell.
Cells of algae; like plant cells they have a cell wall (cellulose) and chloroplasts.
A cell with no nucleus; its DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm (e.g. bacteria).
How many times larger the image is than the real object: image size / real size.

worked.ans: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place, which releases energy. Muscle cells need a lot of energy for contraction, so they have more mitochondria to release more energy.
worked.q: A muscle cell contains many more mitochondria than a skin cell. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.
Aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose.
Muscle cells need lots of energy for contraction, so more mitochondria release more energy.

worked.ans: Cell wall (strengthens/supports), permanent vacuole (cell sap, keeps cell turgid), chloroplasts (photosynthesis).
worked.q: Name three structures found in a palisade leaf cell but not in an animal cell, and give the function of each. (3 marks)
steps: Cell wall: made of cellulose, strengthens and supports the cell.
Permanent vacuole: contains cell sap, keeps the cell turgid.
Chloroplasts: contain chlorophyll, site of photosynthesis.

worked.ans: They have many mitochondria to release energy by aerobic respiration for active transport of mineral ions, but no chloroplasts because there is no light underground for photosynthesis.
worked.q: Explain why root hair cells have mitochondria but no chloroplasts. (3 marks)
steps: Root hair cells take up mineral ions by active transport, which needs energy.
Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration.
Roots are underground and get no light, so chloroplasts (photosynthesis) would be useless.
